Summary:
Quick deep-dive to isolate sources of tail jitter for Peregrine's inference path. Focus on multi-region fanout, KV cache hot-shard behavior, and whether 8-bit/4-bit quantization is worsening p95/p99 under bursty traffic. Demo plan and next steps: run targeted micro-benchmarks, share config and security docs, schedule an on-prem pilot.

Topics:
- Fanout and multi-hop network effects
- KV cache hotkeys / sharding and backpressure
- Streaming vs non-streaming latency tradeoffs
- Quantization latency & kernel selection impacts
- VPC egress/ingress path and on-prem considerations

Action items (recap in meeting): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00:08] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for doing this deep-dive. I know we had some jitter in your staging runs last week, Dana, so we wanted to walk through the whole stack end-to-end.
[00:00:20] Dana (CTO): Yeah, thanks. We're seeing p95 around 120ms which is fine, but p99 spikes to 450ms intermittently. It's unpredictable, sometimes during bursts, sometimes not.
[00:00:29] Liam (SE): Right. Pete — I mean Marcus — when you looked at the traces, do you see network spikes or server-side queuing?
[00:00:36] Marcus (Infra): Mostly server-side queuing on a few hosts. But there are some patterns where requests fan out to a preprocessing service, then to Redwood's runtime, then back through a proxy. So it's multi-hop. We suspect the fanout increases variance.
[00:00:52] Sofia (Redwood Product): We wanted to map that. Fanout can amplify small latencies — if three services are in series, their tail adds up. Also KV cache misses are expensive because we rehydrate large KV segments which can stall.
[00:01:08] Priya (SRE): When KV misses happen we see one worker do a heavy disk read in the on-prem nodes, and that blocks the local queue because of our sync implementation.
[00:01:18] Liam: Got it. A few things I want to call out: (1) batching policy and continuous batching parameters, (2) KV shard placement and whether hot keys are concentrated on single shard, (3) quantization kernel path for short sequences. We often see quantized runs pick slower kernels at certain sequence lengths.
[00:01:36] Ethan (ML Platform): Say more about the kernel path — we're running a custom quant profile with int8 on some models.
[00:01:41] Liam: Sure. In our runtime we have kernel selection heuristics — when the sequence length is below a threshold it uses a different matmul kernel optimized for small matmuls; on other lengths it picks a fused attention kernel. Some quantized kernels are not as vectorized on your GPU, so throughput drops and latency variance increases.
[00:01:59] Marcus: That would explain why shorter prompts sometimes blow up. We have short Q&A calls, 20-40 tokens, and those had the worst spikes.
[00:02:07] Maya: Also, streaming mode changes the critical path: partial outputs flush earlier which reduces tail in some paths but can increase overhead per-token. Non-streamed responses may have lower per-request overhead but larger single latency when model runs longer.
[00:02:21] Dana: We tried toggling streaming on and off in staging. Streaming cut some spikes but introduced CPU overhead on proxy boxes, leading to backpressure and queueing.
[00:02:31] Liam: Right, that's common. Streaming is great for user-perceived latency but if your proxy or edge node doesn't handle many concurrent connections, you get head-of-line issues.
[00:02:41] Priya: Our edge proxy is NGINX+lua. We saw many keep-alives and bursty connection churn.
[00:02:47] Liam: NGINX tuning can help but also consider a lightweight TCP proxy that supports connection pooling.
[00:02:53] [00:03:02] Liam: For KV hotkeys — if a small fraction of keys get >50% of requests, the local shard becomes a hotspot. Our recommendation: introduce a hot-key replication or an LRU local prefix cache, and route writes to multiple replicas during bursts.
[00:03:18] Marcus: We shard by hash across 8 nodes; hot keys still end up on the same hash. Could use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
[00:03:25] Sofia: Also, prefix caching at the runtime level helps — if the same prompt prefixes repeat, we can serve from prefix KV without rehydration. But that uses memory and makes cache eviction policy important.
[00:03:37] Dana: Memory is tight on our on-prem boxes.
[00:03:40] Liam: Then consider a small in-memory hot cache plus a larger remote KV store for cold entries. You trade memory for reduced p99.
[00:03:47] [00:04:12] Marcus: Can quantization be making the variance worse even if average latency improves?
[00:04:17] Liam: Yes. Quantization often improves throughput and mean latency, but if quantized kernels are not well-optimized for your hardware or your sequence lengths, the outliers can get worse. Also, some quantization pathways add occasional dequantize/requantize steps for QA/attention branches that are rare but expensive.
[00:04:34] Ethan: Do you have examples where switching from int8 to int4 increased p99?
[00:04:39] Liam: We've seen that. One customer moved to aggressive int4 and their p50 went down but p99 increased because the int4 fallback kernels used slower tensor cores for some layers.
[00:04:50] Maya: We'll share quant profiles we tested — link: https://redwood.internal/quant-profiles (note: internal shorthand in transcript; actual share will be external link).
[00:05:00] [00:05:26] Dana: On the network side, we saw cross-AZ egress occasionally spike to 30-40ms when our topology caused an extra hop through a centralized gateway. Could that amplify tail?
[00:05:35] Sofia: Absolutely. Each hop contributes its p95/p99. If a route goes through an egress firewall or NAT gateway, it adds variance. For strict p99 SLOs you'd want regional routing and minimal fanout.
[00:05:48] Marcus: We also have intermittent VPN rekeying on the on-prem to cloud tunnel which causes brief packet drops. That aligned with two of our biggest spikes.
[00:05:57] Priya: Ops wants to know if Redwood's private deployment can be fully air-gapped — we have compliance needs.
[00:06:03] Maya: Yes, Redwood Private can run in a VPC or on-prem air-gapped mode. We'll send the deployment checklist and the KMS/HSM integration guide.
[00:06:12] [00:06:45] Liam: Let's brainstorm mitigations grouped by source: network, KV, runtime/quant, proxy. For network: reduce hops, localize model serving, use UDP-based health checks, and tune keepalives. For KV: replicate hot keys, use async rehydrate, and backpressure shedding. For runtime: tune batching window, adjust continuous-batching thresholds, and select kernels via sequence-length profiling. For proxy: connection pooling and streaming multiplexing.
[00:07:10] Marcus: For async rehydrate — is that supported? Right now our implementation blocks the request until KV loaded.
[00:07:16] Liam: We have an async path where the runtime can return a small positive token indicating "pending" and continue when KV is ready; the caller then polls or uses a push hook. It's more complicated for synchronous HTTP APIs but doable with a small state machine.
[00:07:30] Priya: That would reduce head-of-line blockage.
[00:07:32] Maya: Also, consider graceful degradation: fallback to a lower-parameter model variant when KV miss rate is high, or when per-host queue depth exceeds threshold.
[00:07:44] [00:08:10] Ethan: About batching — we saw our default batch size is 64 on dedicated nodes. During low traffic that increases latency, and during burst traffic it sometimes leads to queueing.
[00:08:19] Liam: Adaptive batching may help — expand batch size when throughput is good, shrink it when latency needs tighten. Also continuous batching helps short sequences by aggregating them into micro-batches. But continuous batching needs low variance in arrival patterns or else you introduce wait time.
[00:08:34] Dana: Is there a way to measure whether the kernel selection is causing the p99?
[00:08:38] Liam: Yes, we recommend a profiling run that pins sequence lengths and records kernel selection per layer + timing. Our perf script will output a per-layer histogram. We'll include that script in the benchmark package.
[00:08:51] [00:09:05] Liam: We'll also instrument KV access latencies correlated with request IDs so you can see if every p99 maps to a KV tail.
[00:09:12] Marcus: That'll help.
[00:09:16] [00:09:40] Maya: Quick note on streaming vs non-streaming: in our experience, streaming reduces perceived latency for short outputs but increases protocol overhead and connection pressure. If you have constrained proxies, non-streaming with a smaller batching window can be better.
[00:09:57] Priya: We might move to gRPC at the edge to reduce HTTP overhead. Thoughts?
[00:10:03] Liam: gRPC can help with multiplexing and keepalive efficiency. It reduces cost per-connection compared to many short HTTP streams. But it requires changes on both sides.
[00:10:10] [00:10:40] Dana: Can Redwood do a short on-prem pilot to reproduce our spikes?
[00:10:44] Maya: Yes — we can ship a benchmarking container and a small cluster configuration for your infra team to run. The plan: (1) run baseline with existing config, (2) run with prefix caching + replicated hotkeys, (3) run with different quant profiles (int8 vs int4), (4) run streaming vs non-streaming. We'll compare p50/p95/p99 and throughput.
[00:11:07] Sofia: We'll also provide a topology checklist to highlight potential added hops and NAT/firewall bottlenecks.
[00:11:14] [00:11:45] Marcus: One more thing, we saw tail spikes correlate with nightly backups and some cron jobs. Could noisy neighbors be impacting GPU availability?
[00:11:53] Liam: If the GPUs are shared or if the OS scheduler is pre-empting GPU work for host maintenance, yes. On Dedicated we reserve nodes, but on shared we use Nice scheduling and QOS. We'll check traceroutes and host-level metrics.
[00:12:10] Priya: For resource isolation on-prem, any suggestions?
[00:12:14] Liam: Pin processes to GPUs, isolate NUMA nodes, and ensure disk IO for KV doesn't compete with eviction. Using a local NVMe cache for hot KV reduces disk contention.
[00:12:26] [00:12:40] Dana: Let's recap next steps.
[00:12:44] Maya: Recap: we'll send the benchmark artifacts and quant notes. Liam will produce the micro-benchmarks for KV and kernel profiling. Peregrine will run the pilot and share results. We'll sync in one week.
[00:12:57] Dana: Great, thanks.

Meeting end.
